name: Diego Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and build timber decking and accessible ramps on building sites, currently at a health centre. My vocational trade certificate got me started, and I'm an experienced fitter on a normal trade wage, not a crew boss. I like making an entrance easy to use; my knees notice the long days of carrying boards.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works at a garden centre and our children are grown. We have about four months of expenses saved and some similar builders nearby, with retirement in sight if our income works. I use AI daily for material lists, but measure the doorway myself; I hope to work until about 68 if my knees and the finances allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the decking crew the AI materials list can spare us a trip to the yard, but the ramp still needs to meet the real doorway. Small help is still help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay is the normal trade rate and my partner works at a garden centre. We have four months of expenses saved, our children are grown, and I hope to work until about 68 if my knees and the retirement figures permit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep building the accessible ramps at the health centre and use my daily AI list to order boards, checking lengths against the measured doorway. My partner and I will put a little from each full paid month into a new reserve while site hours and garden-centre wages hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about keeping the work. I like a tool that saves time without pretending it knows what a crooked threshold looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the AI list miss a site detail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AI list chose the standard ramp length, but the door swing needed another hand's width. I measured it twice and changed the board order before cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What money would build the new reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would add forty from future full paid months, after our normal bills. The four months already in our account are the starting point, not new saving.

say: **AI board lists** save trips, while ramps still need doorway measurements.
A small **ordering gain** leaves our site job intact.
think: My **ordinary trade wage** and partner's work cover current bills.
Four months of **savings** gives us room while we check retirement later.
do: **Build** health-centre ramps and check daily AI board lengths against doorways.
**Add** forty from each full paid month if both household wages hold.
feel: **Calm** about familiar paid work and a useful everyday tool.
S0.quote: The AI list chose the standard ramp length, but the door swing needed another hand's width.
fieldNote: He uses **AI daily** for board orders but measures the actual door swing before cutting.
His **new saving** comes from future full paid months while both wages hold, separate from the existing four-month reserve.

steps.text: Build health-centre ramps and check daily AI board lengths
Add forty from future full paid month if both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI will handle more plans and bookings before robots build ramps. If the office changes the board list, I want the worker at the doorway able to change it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My carpentry hours look safe while most changes stay on a screen, and there are some other builders nearby. I worry the new planner could leave us waiting for a board and make the day run past my partner's shift end, but I don't expect a pay cut yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll try the new AI layout controls on an empty ramp bay and learn how to change the slope and board list. I'll compare the result with a tape and level before it becomes a live order, then show the crew which edits worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a digital plan reaching the saw too soon, though my wage feels secure. I like learning a new control while nobody is waiting to use the ramp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you measure before accepting a layout?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mark the doorway height and the slope on the actual slab, then correct the program's board count. A ramp drawing cannot feel the step that catches a wheelchair wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use an empty bay for the first trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd choose an empty bay because there is no patient using it and no other trade has fixed a finish against it. If the tool fails the level check, the measured drawing wins.

say: **AI planning** can help before robots make physical ramps.
The site worker needs **edit control** over doorway and slope measurements.
think: My **carpentry wage** looks safe during office changes.
A wrong **board order** could lengthen the day, though local builders offer some options.
do: **Learn** new AI ramp-layout controls on an empty bay.
**Check** edited slope and board list against tape and level before ordering.
feel: **Uneasy** about digital errors, with current wages still safe.
S1.quote: A ramp drawing cannot feel the step that catches a wheelchair wheel.
fieldNote: He starts **new AI learning** on an empty bay and verifies it with a tape and level before live ordering.
The concern is **schedule disruption**, not a claimed immediate wage cut to his own work.

steps.text: Learn new AI ramp layout controls on empty site bay
Check edited slope and boards against measured tape and level

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 may design the ramps, and capable robots around 2031 could build them. We need to know which paid jobs remain, especially for fitters who cannot stop working at 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about 63 when robots can handle the physical build, five years before the age I hope to leave site work. Four months saved and some nearby builders help, but a cut in ramp shifts would still put our household income and retirement plan under pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the contractor for robot trial dates and paid crew numbers. If a funded, recognised site-machine course offers an actual place with full wages during class, I'll enrol and attend; if my hours are cut first, I'll apply only to posted local construction roles with safe duties, regular hours and pay that covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a wage gap before 68, but ready to learn if the place is real. Our four months of savings buy a pause after a ramp shift cut, not five years of income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner about retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner we should compare retirement statements with our bills before choosing an exit date. I would not ask our grown children to make up a wage we lost at the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should a robot ramp trial include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trial should build a ramp with a real uneven threshold and someone able to stop the robot. An empty showroom floor would miss the part our crew spends time fixing.

say: **2028 thinking AI** designs ramps before robots build them around 2031.
The contractor should publish **paid crew numbers** before site hours change.
think: At about **63**, a ramp-shift cut could precede my hoped-for exit by five years.
Four months of **savings** and some local jobs cannot fund that whole gap.
do: **Ask** contractor for robot trial dates and paid crew numbers this week.
**Enrol** in funded recognised site-machine course if real place and full class wages offered.
**Apply** after cuts to posted local construction job with safe duties and regular bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about possible income loss, with a funded learning route.
S2.quote: Our four months of savings buy a pause after a ramp shift cut, not five years of income.
fieldNote: He needs wages until roughly **68 if finances permit**, so robots at about 63 pose a credible gap.
Training needs **funded fees**, full wages and a real place; applications need posted local work with safe duties and adequate pay.

steps.text: Ask contractor for robot trial dates and paid crew numbers
Enrol in funded recognised site-machine course if real place and full class wages offered
Apply after cuts to posted local construction job with safe duties and regular bill-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 changes the drawings, and robots around 2034 could put the ramps in. Five years lets us test a machine on a real slope and get workers trained before the site routine changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about 66 when robots do the fitting, still before my hoped-for exit around 68. If the work is cut then, the four-month cushion cannot cover two working years and a delayed retirement decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll enrol this winter in a free evening introduction to machine safety while keeping my ramp job. I'll ask the contractor to fund the recognised site-equipment certificate with paid assessment days; if it confirms a place, fees and wages in writing, I'll enrol next intake, then apply to a posted local equipment-checking role only if my ramp shifts are cut and the job pays enough for our bills with safe hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible two-year pay gap, with enough warning to learn. The free class is a first step, not a promised equipment job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must a useful machine lesson include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want an instructor to show how to stop the machine on an uneven ramp, then have me do it. A lesson behind a barrier will not teach me to stop a site robot on an uneven ramp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an equipment-checking job worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the posted wage, weekly hours and whether I can do the lifting safely. If there is no real equipment-checking vacancy at adequate pay, I'll keep looking while I have a ramp wage.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes plans before robots build ramps around 2034.
A **real-slope trial** and paid worker training should come first.
think: At about **66**, a lost ramp wage could precede my hoped-for exit at 68.
The **four-month cushion** cannot carry a two-year gap alone.
do: **Attend** free evening machine-safety introduction this winter while employed.
**Enrol** in recognised certificate if written funded place and paid assessment days secured.
**Apply** after certificate and ramp cuts to posted local equipment job with safe bill-covering hours.
feel: **Anxious** about possible wages lost before affordable retirement.
S3.quote: A lesson behind a barrier will not teach me to stop a site robot on an uneven ramp.
fieldNote: He starts **actual free learning** now and sets written fee, place and paid assessment conditions for a recognised certificate.
Any equipment application follows **an actual ramp-shift cut** and needs a posted local role with safe hours and bill-covering wages.

steps.text: Enrol in recognised equipment certificate if written funded place and paid assessment days secured
Apply after certificate and ramp cuts to posted local equipment job with safe bill-covering hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2036 may plan ramps and capable robots around 2039 may build them. I hope to have stopped regular site work around 68 if our retirement numbers allow it, so this is mostly a handover question for younger fitters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about 71 when the robots can do hands-on work, beyond the age I hope to leave the site. We have four months saved now, not a guaranteed retirement income, so my partner and I still need to check the actual figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the ramp safety ticket current while I am working and review retirement income with my partner each year. If the figures support leaving around 68, I'll hand the doorway measurements and slope checks to a younger fitter before my last job; if they do not, I will look at posted local light-duty site roles with regular bill-covering pay rather than assume I can work through 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the retirement arithmetic, though the decade keeps capable robots beyond my hoped-for work period. I can prepare a handover without pretending the exit is certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach the next ramp fitter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a younger fitter to measure the rise from the actual doorway and check it with a level. A ramp can meet a digital slope and still leave a lip that catches a wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would light-duty work become an option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A light-duty role would need a real local posting, a clear wage, regular hours and lifting that my knees can manage. I would only apply if our retirement figures are short and a suitable role actually exists.

say: **2036 thinking AI** plans ramps before robots build them around 2039.
A **measured handover** matters if I leave regular site work around 68.
think: At about **71**, robots may arrive after my hoped-for exit, if income permits.
Our **four-month reserve** is not proof that retirement costs are covered.
do: **Keep** ramp safety ticket current while on present site rota.
**Review** retirement income against bills with partner each year.
**Apply** if retirement income short to posted local light-duty job with safe bill-covering pay.
feel: **Uneasy** about affordability, with time for a conditional handover.
S4.quote: A ramp can meet a digital slope and still leave a lip that catches a wheel.
fieldNote: He speaks of **2039 as later** than his hoped-for work, conditional on income, without claiming he remains employed at 71.
Any later application needs **short retirement income** and a posted local role with regular hours, safe lifting and bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Keep ramp safety ticket current on present site rota
Review retirement income with partner against household bills yearly
Apply if income short to posted local light-duty job with safe regular bill-covering pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because ramp robots around 2031 could cut shifts when I would be about 63, years before I hope to stop. A paid equipment course, real local roles with safe duties and honest crew figures would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the threshold after a robot builds a ramp. A wheelchair wheel finds the small lip that a drawing leaves out. I want the next fitter taught to test the entrance before people use it.

headlineQuote: A wheelchair wheel finds the small lip that a drawing leaves out.
portrait: **Diego**, 58, fits ramps and decking with a vocational trade certificate, typical pay and experienced site skills.
His garden-centre partner and grown children share a **four-month reserve**, with some nearby building jobs available.
He uses **AI daily** for materials and learns new controls early, while his knees make safe duties important.
Fast robots make him **anxious** about wages before his hoped-for conditional exit around 68; slower change supports study and handover.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring ramp robots around 2031 when he would be about 63 and may need wages.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid equipment course**, real local roles with safe duties and honest crew figures would help him plan.
